At first I couldn’t bear school, but after a while I learnt to stand it. When I got extra tired of it I played hookey, and the whipping I caught next morning done me good and brightened me up. So school got easier the longer I kept going. I was growing used to the widow’s notions, too, and they didn’t scrape on me so much. I still preferred the old ways, though I was beginning to like the new ones a small amount. The widow said my progress was slow but certain, and she was well satisfied. I would sing ‘sul margine d’un rio,’ my father’s favourite song, and my voice, floating through the still air, would tell him, in whatever shaded retreat he waited for our reunion, that his daughter had arrived. By then the mark of suffering would have disappeared from my forehead, and I would lift my eyes fearlessly to his, which always shone with the gentle brightness of innocent love. Remembering the magical expression of those deep eyes, I wept—but softly, afraid my sobs might disturb the enchanted scene.

I was so completely absorbed in this vision that I walked on without watching my steps. Only when I actually bent to pick a flower for my wreath, on that barren plain where no flowers grew, did I wake from my daydream and discover that I had no idea where I was.

The sun had set, and the rosy colour it had left on the clouds as it descended had almost faded. Wind swept across the plain. I looked around but saw nothing to tell me my location; I was lost, and tried unsuccessfully to find my path. I continued wandering, while the gathering darkness blurred every trace that might have guided me. At last everything disappeared into the deep obscurity of a pitch-black night. I grew tired, and knew that my servant was spending the night in the neighbouring village, so no one would be alarmed by my absence. I also knew that in this desolate place I was safe from any intruder, and I decided to stay where I was until morning. Indeed, I was too exhausted to walk any farther. The air was cold, but I cared little for physical discomfort, and thought myself thoroughly accustomed to the weather after two years of solitude, during which no change of season had interrupted my constant wandering.

I lay on the grass in darkness untouched by even the faintest ray of light. There was no sound: the deep night had put the insects to sleep, and they were the only creatures living in this lonely place, where neither tree nor shrub offered shelter to anything else.
